If vs. Unless in the Real Conditional

You use the Real Conditional to express events or situations that are likely to happen.
You use If or unless to express conditions for the events to occur.
Unless is used in conditional sentences as a necessary condition without which the outcome of the sentence can't happen.

Example:
You can't keep up unless you are connected.
If ... not is used when the outcome in the if clause is unexpected or in questions.

Examples:
It will be surprising if this doesn't continue.
If you don't have access to the Internet, what will you do?
You can't keep up unless you are connected.
If you don't have access in this scenario, what will you do?
Unless the price of these innovations comes down, they will remain forever out of reach.
It will be surprising if this doesn't continue as each new item is rolled out for consumption.
Identifying the Main Ideas of a Text
When you read a text, it's important to identify the main ideas that you find.
When you want to identify the main ideas of a text, try to answer the following questions:

• What/Who?
What or who is the text talking about?

• How?
How does the text convey its message?

• When/Where/Why?
What are the details or supporting arguments that you can find in the text?
Read the following paragraph and notice how the expressions in bold answer these questions.
What exactly is the digital divide? (what?)
It is an economic and social equality tied to the ability to have access to information and communication technology. (what?)

This means computers and internet connectivity. In the U.S. this divide may be between households, businesses or geographic areas. Globally, it refers to the technological gap between developing and developed countries. (where?)
You can't keep up unless you are connected. (who?)
In the beginning, when North American and Europe moved to a more computer and Internet-based life, they left everyone not connected behind, both within their borders and without. (when?/who?/where?)
Write a 10 question survey about digital devices people have.
Find out about cell phones, computers, printers, notebooks and types of internet service people have.
Also find out how much the devices are used, how long they are used per day and by whom.
Ask 10 to 15 people all of the questions.
Combine your results with a partner's results.
Write sentences to report your findings in percentages.
Share your results with the class.
Decide as a group whether there are or not any digital divides.

images.text: What exactly is the digital divide? It is an economic and social equality tied to the ability to have access to information and communication technology. This means computers and internet connectivity. In the U.S. this divide may be between households, businesses or geographic areas. Globally, it refers to the technological gap between developing and developed countries. You can't keep up unless you are connected.

In the beginning, when North America and Europe moved to a more computer and internet based life, they left everyone who was not connected behind, both within their borders and without. If you don't have access in this scenario, what will you do? Many had to survive without.
North Americans found computers where they could. They were encouraged to buddy up with someone with a computer to do schoolwork. As levels of connectivity grew, more women, racial and ethnic minorities, lower income and rural residents, and less educated people gained access. They seemed to catch up, at least in the short term.

Recent studies now look at the digital divide in terms of bandwidth. DSL, cable modems and WiFi increased the level of inequality once again. "How?" you may wonder. If these weren't only available to a portion of society to begin with, they would not. Unless the price of these innovations comes down, they will remain forever out of reach.
It will be surprising if this doesn't continue as each new item is rolled out for consumption. The truth is, that unless people have the money to pay for access, know how to use the tools and understand the information available, they will always remain behind.
So, the divide persists. If it wasn't the outcome we wanted, it still what we have, at least for now. Let's hope things change.
